title: Dimensional modelling
description: Facts in the centre. Context around them. A visual guide to Kimball concepts.

sections.title: Start with the business question
sections.body: The most useful starting point is not a table. It is the question you want to answer. “I want to analyse sales by customer, product, store and date” already tells you the shape of the model.
sections.callout: Facts answer “what happened / how much?” Dimensions answer “who / what / where / when / why?”

sections.title: A clearer modelling workflow
sections.body: The order matters because the grain is the contract that keeps every later decision honest.

steps.title: Choose a process
steps.text: Sales, orders, shipments, claims, sessions or marketing impressions.

steps.title: Declare the grain
steps.text: State exactly what one fact row means: one row per product on one transaction.

steps.title: Identify dimensions
steps.text: What will users filter, group or slice by? Date, customer, product, channel, promotion.

steps.title: Identify facts
steps.text: What numeric measurements are valid at that grain? Units, revenue, cost, discount.

sections.title: What goes where?
sections.body: A fact table records an event at a declared grain. Dimensions hold the descriptive context that makes the event useful to analyse.

sections.title: The dimension becomes the flat table
sections.body: Kimball is not saying the fact becomes a dimension. Descriptive hierarchies are usually flattened into a wide dimension so an analyst can filter product → category → department without walking a chain of joins.
sections.callout: In BigQuery, a denormalised dimension often makes the common analytical query simpler and avoids repeated joins through small lookup tables.

sections.title: Conformed dimensions create a shared language
sections.body: A conformed dimension is reused consistently by multiple business processes. Sales and returns can both use the same product definition, so “category” means the same thing in both analyses.

sections.title: How this maps to your work
sections.body: For marketing decisioning, the event might be an impression or a customer session. The grain has to be explicit before calculating response rate, attribution or uplift.
sections.callout: Example grain: one row per customer × offer × impression timestamp. Customer, offer, channel and date are dimensions; impressed, clicked, converted and value are facts.
